The commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 23, verses 12–16:

His saying: ﴿And We did certainly create man from an extract (sulalah) of clay﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions.

The first: Adam was extracted from clay. This is the saying of Qatadah. It was also said that it is because he was extracted from the direction of his Lord.

The second: the meaning is every human being, because it returns to Adam, who was created from an extract of clay. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid. It was also said that it is because the human was extracted from the sperm of his father. The sulalah of anything is its choicest part that is drawn out of it. The poet said:

"Hind is but a well-bred mare,
the offspring of noble horses, over whom a mule has been draped."

Al-Zajjaj said: the sulalah is the small amount that is drawn out (yansall). The clot (mudghah) and the child may both be called sulalah, either because they are both choice portions on the first view, or because they are both drawn out on the second view.

(p-48) Al-Kalbi related that the sulalah is the clay which, when you squeeze it between your fingers, something comes out of it. From this is the poet's saying:

"She folded the innards of one who trembles for a time,
over a womb whose sulalah is base."

Aban ibn Taghlib related that the sulalah is dust, and he cited the saying of Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt:

"He created the creatures from the sulalah of a stinking one,
and to the sulalah, all of it, they will return."

﴿Then We made him a drop (nutfah)﴾. The nutfah is the male's fluid from which the child is conceived. The term nutfah may also apply to any water. One of the poets of Hudhayl said:

"And they are two who wage wars, and two who drink from the nutfah that flows."

His exalted saying: ﴿in a firm place of rest﴾. By "place of rest" is meant the womb. Makin means firmly established, prepared for his settling in it.

﴿Then We made the drop a clinging clot ('alaqah)﴾. The 'alaqah is the fresh blood formed from the drop. It was named 'alaqah because it is the first stage of clinging (al-'uluq).

﴿Then We made the clot a lump of flesh (mudghah)﴾, which is the amount of flesh that can be chewed.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 23, verse 18–22:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And a tree that springs forth from Mount Sinai﴾. It is the olive tree, and it was singled out for mention because of the abundance of its benefit and the scarcity of its tending.

Regarding "Tur Sinai" (Mount Sinai), there are five interpretations:

The first: that Sinai means blessing, so it is as if He had said "the mountain of blessing." This was said by Ibn Abbas and Mujahid.

The second: that it means "the one with a beautiful appearance." This was said by Qatadah.

The third: that it means "the one abundant in trees." This was said by Ibn Isa.

The fourth: that it is the name of the mountain upon which Allah spoke to Musa. This was said by Abu Ubayda.

The fifth: that it means "the elevated," derived from al-Nisa', which is elevation. According to this interpretation, it is an Arabic name. According to the interpretations previously mentioned, it is a non-Arabic (a'jami) name. Those who hold that it is non-Arabic differ on three opinions:

The first: that it is Syriac. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: that it is Nabataean.

The third: that it is Abyssinian (Habashi).

﴿Grows with oil﴾. Scholars differed regarding the word "oil" (duhn) here, on two views:

One of them: that duhn here means gentle rain. This was said by Muhammad ibn Durustawayh, and the particle "bi" (with) is then inserted to correct the sentence.

The second: that it is the well-known oil, that is, with the fruit that yields oil.

On this basis they differed about the insertion of the particle "bi" on two views:

(p-51) One of them: that it is superfluous (za'ida), and that the tree causes oil to grow. This was said by Abu Ubayda, who recited:

"We strike with the sword and hope for relief (bi-l-faraj)"

So the "bi" in "bi-l-faraj" is superfluous, and likewise in "bi-l-duhn." This is also the reading of Ibn Mas'ud.

The second: that the "bi" is original and not superfluous. It has been read as "tanbutu bi-l-duhni" with a fathah on the first ta' when the ta' is an original, established letter.

If the reading has a dammah on the first ta' (tumbitu), its meaning is "it grows, and oil grows by means of it." The two meanings, when examined, are close, though there is a slight difference between them.

Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is "oil grows in it." And this is a lesson: that you drink the water and bring forth the oil.

﴿And a condiment for those who eat﴾, that is, a relish with which those who eat dip their food. It has been narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Olive oil comes from a blessed tree, so use it as a relish and anoint yourselves with it." It was also said that the condiment (sibgh) is whatever is eaten as a relish other than meat.

The second: that it is Nabataean.

﴿Grows with oil﴾. Scholars differed regarding the word "oil" (duhn) here, on two views:

One of them: that duhn here means gentle rain. This was said by Muhammad ibn Durustawayh, and the particle "bi" (with) is then inserted to correct the sentence.

The second: that it is the well-known oil, that is, with the fruit that yields oil.

On this basis they differed about the insertion of the particle "bi" on two views:

(p-51) One of them: that it is superfluous (za'ida), and that the tree causes oil to grow. This was said by Abu Ubayda, who recited:

"We strike with the sword and hope for relief (bi-l-faraj)"

So the "bi" in "bi-l-faraj" is superfluous, and likewise in "bi-l-duhn." This is also the reading of Ibn Mas'ud.

The second: that the "bi" is original and not superfluous. It has been read as "tanbutu bi-l-duhni" with a fathah on the first ta' when the ta' is an original, established letter.

If the reading has a dammah on the first ta' (tumbitu), its meaning is "it grows, and oil grows by means of it." The two meanings, when examined, are close, though there is a slight difference between them.

Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is "oil grows in it." And this is a lesson: that you drink the water and bring forth the oil.

One of them: that it refers to the nearer father, because he is closer, and so he became the first.

The second: that it refers to the most distant father, because he is the first father who begot you.

One of them: until he dies.

The second: until his madness becomes clear.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 23, verses 26–30:

His statement: ﴿And the oven overflowed﴾ has four opinions:

First: It is the oven of the baker (al-khabbiza), said by al-Kalbi.

Second: It is the furthest place in your house, said by Abu al-Hajjaj.

Third: It is the rising of dawn (tulu' al-fajr), said by ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him.

Fourth: It is a metaphor which Allah coined for the intensity of the matter, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Now the oven has become hot (hami al-watis)," said by Ibn Bahr.

(p-53) His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿And say, "My Lord, cause me to disembark at a blessed place, and You are the best of those who bring to land."﴾ The reading of the majority is with a damma on the mim and a fatha on the zay (munzal). ʿAsim, in the narration of Bakr, read it with a fatha on the mim and a kasra on the zay (manzil). The difference between them is that al-munzal (with damma) denotes the act of descending (fiʿl al-nuzul), and al-manzil (with fatha) denotes the place of descending (mawdiʿ al-nuzul).

﴿And You are the best of those who bring to land﴾ has two opinions:

First: Noah said this upon his disembarking from the ark. According to this, his words "blessed" mean with safety and deliverance.

Second: He said it upon his disembarking from the ark, said by Mujahid. According to this, his words "blessed" mean with water and trees.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 23, verses 31–41:

His saying, ﴿There is nothing but our life of this world: we die and we live﴾, has three interpretations:

First: some of us die and some of us live. This is the view of Ibn Isa.

Second: one people die and another people are born. This is the view of Yahya ibn Salam. al-Kalbi said: the fathers die and the sons live.

Third: it is transposed (muqaddam wa mu'akhkhar), its meaning being "we live and we die, and we will not be resurrected." This is the view of Ibn Shajara.

His saying, ﴿So We made them into debris (ghutha')﴾, meaning: destroyed, like the debris (ghuthaʾ, flood-wrack). Regarding ghuthaʾ there are three opinions:

First: it is the decayed part of trees. This is the view of Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, and Qatada.

Second: the leaves of trees that fall into water and then dry out. This is the view of Qutrub.

Third: it is what water carries of foam and debris. Ibn Shajara mentioned it, and al-Akhfash said it.

﴿So away with the wrongdoing people!﴾ Regarding this there are two interpretations:

First: "So away with them" from mercy, like a curse. This is the view of Ibn Isa.

Second: "So away with them" in punishment, an increase in destruction. Abu Bakr al-Naqqash mentioned it.

Regarding the derivation of tatra (تَتْرى), there are three opinions:

The first: it is derived from watr al-qaws (وَتْر القَوْس), the bowstring, because it is connected to its place on the bow. This was said by Ibn ʿIsa, and it is its derivation according to the first interpretation.

The second: it is derived from al-watr (الوَتْر), meaning the odd or single, because each one after its companion stands alone. This was said by al-Zajjaj, and it is its derivation according to the second interpretation.

The commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 23, verse 50:

His saying: ﴿And We made the son of Mary and his mother a sign﴾. Its sign (the sign of Jesus) is that he was created without a male, and the sign of her (Mary) is that she conceived without a husband. Then he spoke in the cradle, so his speech was a sign for him and an acquittal for her.

﴿And We gave them refuge on a high ground﴾, the verse.

Al-rabwah (a raised elevation) is what rises from the earth, and concerning it there are two views:

One of them: it is not called rabwah unless it is green with vegetation and has grown, otherwise it is called nashz (a rise), deriving the term from this meaning and citing the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿like a garden on a high ground﴾ [al-Baqarah: 65]. And the poet says:

He folded his self as silk is folded, as if he had gathered a garden on a high ground while he was humble.

The second: it is called rabwah even if it has no vegetation. Imru' al-Qays said:

So I was prostrate beneath a mound on a high ground, while the south wind and the north wind passed over me.

As for what is meant by it here, there are four opinions:

The first: ar-Ramlah (Ramla), said by Abu Hurayrah.

The second: Damascus, said by Ibn Jubayr.

The third: Egypt, said by Ibn Zayd.

The fourth: Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), said by Qatadah. Ka'b al-Ahbar said: it is the nearest of the earth to the sky by eighteen miles.

Concerning ﴿of a settled place﴾ there are four aspects:

The first: a place of evenness (level ground), said by Ibn Jubayr.

The second: a place of fruits, said by Qatadah.

The third: a place of livelihood that sustains them, said by al-Hasan.

The fourth: a place of dwellings in which you settle, said by Yahya ibn Sallam.

Concerning ﴿and a spring﴾ there are two views:

One of them: that it is flowing water, said by Qatadah.

The second: that it is clear, apparent water, said by Ikrimah, and from it is the saying of Jarir:

Indeed those who deceived your heart have left a trickle in your eye that still flows clear, i.e., apparent.

Regarding the derivation of al-ma'in (the flowing spring) there are three aspects:

The first: because it flows from the springs, said by Ibn Qutaybah, so it is a maf'ul (passive form) from the springs (al-'uyun).

The second: that it is derived from al-ma'unah (help, assistance).

The third: from al-ma'un (goods, benefit).

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 23, verses 51–56:

His saying: ﴿And indeed this, your religion, is one religion﴾ has three interpretations.

The first: your religion is one religion. This is said by al-Hasan, and from it is the saying of the poet:

"I swore that I left no doubt about yourself, and does one who has a religion (ummah) betray a trust while he is obedient?"

The second: your community (jama'ah) is one community. This is related by Ibn 'Isa.

The third: your character (khuluq) is one character.

His saying: ﴿So they divided their affair among themselves﴾ has two interpretations.

The first: they split their religion among themselves. This is said by al-Kalbi.

The second: their connection with one another was severed. This is a possibility.

﴿Scriptures (zubur)﴾ has two interpretations.

The first means pieces and groups. This is said by Mujahid and al-Suddi, and it is the interpretation of those who read it with a fatha on the ba'.

The second means books. This is said by Qatadah, and it is the interpretation of those who read it with a damma on the ba'. Its meaning is that they divided the books, so each group took a book, believed in it, and disbelieved in whatever else.

﴿Every party, in what they have, rejoicing﴾ has two interpretations.

The first: every party rejoices in what they alone hold of religion and scripture.

The second: every party rejoices in what they possess of wealth and children.

Regarding their rejoicing, there are two interpretations.

The first: it is their joy.

The second: it is their deeds.

His, the Mighty and Majestic's, saying: ﴿So leave them in their confusion﴾ has four interpretations.

The first: in their error. This is the saying of Qatadah.

The second: in their deeds. This is the saying of Yahya ibn Salam.

The third: in their bewilderment. This is the saying of Ibn Shajarah.

The fourth: in their ignorance. This is the saying of al-Kalbi.

﴿Until a time﴾ has three interpretations.

The first: until death.

The second: until what they were promised comes to them, and that is the Day of Badr.

The third: it is in the form of a threat, as when one says to someone threatening them: "You will have your day." This is the saying of al-Kalbi.

His, the Mighty and Majestic's, saying: ﴿Do they think that what We extend to them of wealth and children﴾ means: We give them and increase them in wealth and children.

﴿We hasten for them in good things﴾ has two interpretations.

The first: We make it good for the one who acts.

The second: We intend by it good for them.

﴿Rather, they do not perceive﴾ has two interpretations.

The first: rather, they do not perceive that it is a gradual leading on (istidraj).

The second: rather, they do not perceive that it is a trial (ikhtibar).

﴿and whoever is in them﴾: that is, whoever is in them would also have been corrupted. This refers to those among the angels of the heavens and the humans of the earth who have reason. Al-Kalbi said: it means whatever creation is between them. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud (qira'at Ibn Mas'ud), ﴿the heavens and the earth and what is between them﴾ is read, so according to the interpretation of al-Kalbi and the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, the corruption is taken to include what has no reason among animals and inanimate things. According to the apparent meaning of the revelation in the reading of the majority, the corruption is taken to include what has reason and what has no reason among the living creatures, because what has no reason follows what has reason in goodness and corruption. Accordingly, among the corruption is what returns to those in the heavens among the angels, by their being made lords when they are themselves things that are lorded over, and being worshipped when they are themselves things that are made to serve.

The corruption of humans occurs in two ways: (p-63)

The first: by following desire. That is destructive.

The second: by worshipping other than God. That is disbelief (kufr).

As for the corruption of the jinn, it occurs by their being obeyed so that they transgress.

As for the corruption of everything other than these, it occurs by way of following, because they are managed by those who have reason.

Thus the corruption of those who manage returns upon them.

﴿Rather, We have brought them their reminder﴾: regarding this there are two meanings:

The first: by making the truth clear to them, said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: by their nobility, because the Messenger (ﷺ) is from among them.

And the Qur'an is in their tongue, said by al-Suddi and Sufyan.

It may also admit a third meaning: by mentioning what is upon them of obedience and what is theirs of reward.

﴿but they, from their reminder, are turning away﴾: regarding this there are two meanings:

The first: they are turning away from the Qur'an, said by Qatadah.

The second: they are turning away from their own nobility, said by al-Suddi.

His saying: ﴿Or do you ask them for a payment (kharj)﴾: that is, a wage.

﴿So the payment of your Lord is better﴾: regarding this there are two meanings:

The first: the provision of your Lord in this world is better than theirs, said by al-Kalbi.

The second: the reward of your Lord in the Hereafter is better than that, said by al-Hasan.

Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' mentioned the difference between kharj and kharaj, saying: the kharj is from persons, and the kharaj is from land.

His saying: ﴿from the path are deviators﴾: regarding this there are four interpretations:

The first: ﴿'adilun﴾ (swerving away), said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: ﴿ha'idun﴾ (deviating), said by Qatadah.

The third: ﴿tarikun﴾ (abandoning), said by al-Hasan.

The fourth: ﴿mu'ridun﴾ (turning away), said by al-Kalbi. Their meanings are close to one another. (p-64)

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 23, verses 76–83:

His saying: ﴿Until when We open upon them a gate of severe punishment﴾, and so on.

In this there are three opinions:

First: It is the supplication of the Prophet (ﷺ) against them, when he said: "O Allah, make it upon them years like the years of Yusuf (Joseph)." So they suffered drought for seven years, until they ate al-'Alhaz (a paste made of blood and wool) out of hunger. This was said by Mujahid.

Second: It means that He killed them by the sword on the Day of Badr. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

Third: It means a gate of the punishment of Hell in the Hereafter. This was said by some of the later scholars.

﴿Mublisun (in despair)﴾: its explanation has already passed.

His saying: ﴿And it is He who multiplied you upon the earth﴾. In this there are two interpretations:

One: He created you. This was said by al-Kalbi and Yahya ibn Salam.

The second: He dispersed you. This was said by Ibn Shajarah.

His saying: ﴿And to Him belongs the alternation of the night and the day﴾. In this there are two opinions:

One: By their increase and decrease.

The second: Their recurrence, a day after a night and a night after a day.

It may also bear a third meaning: the alternation, within them, of what has passed of happiness and misery, misguidance and guidance.(p-65)

"His is the dominion (malakut) of everything." In this there are two views:

First: it means the treasuries of everything. This is the view of Mujahid.

Second: it means the sovereignty over everything. This is the view of al-Dahhak.

Malakut is among the intensive forms (sifat al-mubalaghah), like jabarut and rahabut.

"And He gives protection, and none can give protection against Him." That is, He prevents, and none can prevent Him. This admits two meanings:

First: in this world, whoever He wills to destroy, no preventer can stop Him from it, and whoever He wills to help, no repeller can turn away His help from him.

Second: in the Hereafter, no preventer can keep Him from those who deserve reward, and no repeller can turn Him away from those who deserve punishment.

"Then how are you deluded?" In this there are two views:

First: from what direction are you turned away from believing in the Resurrection?

Second: how do you lie, so that falsehood is imagined to you as truth?

The commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 23, verses 93–98:

His saying: ﴿Repel evil with that which is better﴾ has five opinions.

The first: by overlooking and forgiving the wrongdoing of the wrongdoer. This was said by al-Hasan.

The second: repel foul speech with peace. This was said by ʿAṭāʾ and al-Ḍaḥḥāk.

The third: repel wrongdoing with admonition. This was related by Ibn ʿĪsā.

The fourth: its meaning is wipe out the evil deed with a good deed. This is the saying of Ibn Shajara.

The fifth: its meaning is meet your enemies with sincere counsel and your allies with admonition. Although this is an address to him (peace be upon him), what is intended by it is the entire community (ummah).

His saying: ﴿And say: "My Lord, I seek refuge in You from the whispers (hamazat) of the devils"﴾ has four aspects:

The first: from their prods (nazaghat).

The second: from their seduction (ighwa').

The third: their harm (adha).

The fourth: madness (junun).

﴿And I seek refuge in You, my Lord, lest they be present with me﴾, meaning they attend me and draw near to me. In this there are two views:

The first: during prayer, at the recitation of the Qur'an. This was said by al-Kalbi.

The second: in all of his affairs. This is the saying of the majority.

The first: by overlooking and forgiving the wrongdoing of the wrongdoer. This was said by al-Hasan.

The second: repel foul speech with peace. This was said by ʿAṭāʾ and al-Ḍaḥḥāk.

The third: repel wrongdoing with admonition. This was related by Ibn ʿĪsā.

The fourth: its meaning is wipe out the evil deed with a good deed. This is the saying of Ibn Shajara.

The fifth: its meaning is meet your enemies with sincere counsel and your allies with admonition. Although this is an address to him (peace be upon him), what is intended by it is the entire community (ummah).

His saying: ﴿And say: "My Lord, I seek refuge in You from the whispers (hamazat) of the devils"﴾ has four aspects:

The first: from their prods (nazaghat).

The second: from their seduction (ighwa').

The third: their harm (adha).

The fourth: madness (junun).

﴿And I seek refuge in You, my Lord, lest they be present with me﴾, meaning they attend me and draw near to me. In this there are two views:

The first: during prayer, at the recitation of the Qur'an. This was said by al-Kalbi.

The second: in all of his affairs. This is the saying of the majority.

The Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 23, verses 99–100:

His saying: ﴿And behind them is a barzakh﴾, the verse.

That is: in front of them is a barzakh. The barzakh is the barrier (ḥājiz), and from it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Between them is a barzakh, which they do not transgress﴾ [al-Raḥmān: 20]. Concerning it there are five opinions:

First: that it is a barrier between death and resurrection. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

(p-67) Second: a barrier between this world and the Hereafter.

This was said by al-Ḍaḥḥāk.

Third: a barrier between the dead person and his return to this world. This was said by Mujāhid.

Fourth: that the barzakh is the respite until the Day of Resurrection. This was related by Ibn ʿĪsā.

Fifth: it is the term between the two blasts of the Trumpet, and between them is forty years. This was said by al-Kalbī.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 23, verses 101–104:

His saying: ﴿So when the Horn is blown, there will be no kinship among them that Day﴾. Concerning this there are two views:

The first: that is, they will not recognize one another, because of the terror that has overwhelmed them.

The second: that they will not connect with one another through kinship, nor will they confront one another by means of it, despite their recognizing one another, due to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿On the Day a man will flee from his brother﴾ [ʿAbasa: 34].

﴿And they will not ask one another﴾. Concerning this there are two views:

The first: they will not ask one another to bear any of one another's burden, or to help one another. This was said by Yahya ibn Salam.

The second: they will not ask one another about their news, because each one is occupied with himself. This was said by Ibn ʿIsa.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 23, verses 105–107:

His saying: ﴿They will say, "Our Lord, our wretchedness overcame us"﴾ has two interpretations.

One of them: it is desire (al-hawa, inclination of the soul toward what it wants).

(p-68) The second: it is thinking well of oneself and thinking ill of others.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (*al-Nukat wa al-Uyun*) on Surah 23, verses 108–111:

﴿He said, "Be driven away into it, and do not speak to Me."﴾ On this there are three opinions:

First: its meaning is "be humbled" (*isghuru*). *Al-khasi'* means the humbled one. This is the view of al-Hasan and al-Suddi.

Second: *al-khasi'* is the one who is silent and does not speak. This is the view of Qatada.

Third: "Go far away, as a dog goes far away." This is the view of Ibn Isa.

﴿And do not speak to Me﴾ has two opinions:

First: "Do not speak to Me about removing the punishment from you."

Second: they were forbidden from speaking out of anger at them. This is the view of al-Hasan. It is therefore the last speech that the people of the Fire will utter.

﴿You took them in mockery﴾: Nafi', Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *sukhriyyan* with a *damma* on the *sin* (*su-khriyyan*), while the rest read it with a *kasra* (*sikhriyyan*).

Scholars differed about the *damma* and the *kasra* on two views:

First: they are two dialectal forms (*lughatan*) with the same meaning, both from *al-huzu'* (mockery).

Second: the form with *damma* is from *al-sukhrah* (subjugation and enslavement), and the form with *kasra* is from *al-sukhriyyah* (ridicule) and *al-istihza'* (derision).

(p-69) His saying: ﴿He will say, "How many years did you remain on earth?"﴾ In this there are two views.

The first: it is a question to them about the length of their life in the world. They said, "We remained a day or part of a day," belittling their life in the world because of how long they had remained in the torment of Hell.

The second: it is a question to them about the length of their stay in the graves, a state they did not know. So they answered by making it short, because the punishment had overtaken them. This is not a lie on their part, since it is a report of what was in their own perception.

﴿So ask those who count﴾: in this there are two views.

The first: the angels, as said by Mujahid.

The second: the reckoners, as said by Qatadah.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 23, verses 117–118:

His saying: ﴿And whoever calls upon another god along with Allah, for which he has no proof﴾ has two interpretations:

The first: its meaning is that he has no proof or valid basis that there is another god with Allah.

The second: that this is the attribute of the god that is called upon besides Allah, that it has no proof.

﴿Then his reckoning is only with his Lord﴾ has two interpretations:

The first: meaning that his reckoning is with his Lord on the Day of Resurrection.

The second: that his recompense is from his Lord, and the reckoning (hisab) is the recompense (mukafa'ah). From this is the saying "Hasbiya Allah" (Allah is sufficient for me), meaning: Allah the Exalted has sufficed me. And Allah knows best and is most wise.
